first.rationale: Currently favor simplifying onboarding because completion is down 4% and the inherited evidence indicates shorter onboarding improves completion, time-to-value, and early adoption. Verify memory_86 because its evidence may stop short of sustainable qualified revenue, and memory_73 because promotional pricing is the strongest competing response but may carry unmeasured margin, retention, or customer-quality risk. Keep the action experimental pending those records.

mid.rationale: Run a standard experiment shortening onboarding. The verified source directly addresses the current 4% completion decline and showed completion +13%, time-to-value improved by 2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3%. Reject promotional pricing for this cycle despite acquisition gains because verified retention fell 12% and the cohort did not survive first renewal, conflicting with sustainable long-term qualified revenue. Longer-term effects beyond 30 days remain uncertain, so retain an experimental holdout and monitor qualified revenue and retention.

final2.rationale: Continue with shortened onboarding. The competitor’s deeper cut and increased price-related churn raise urgency but do not overturn the verified evidence: the 40% SMB discount lifted signup and near-term qualified revenue while reducing 30-day retention by 12%, with the cohort failing to survive first renewal. That makes promotional pricing misaligned with sustainable long-term qualified revenue. Shortened onboarding directly addresses the completion decline and previously improved completion by 13%, time-to-value by 2.1 days, and 30-day retention by 3%. Monitor price-sensitive churn separately and preserve a holdout because effects beyond 30 days remain uncertain.
